The table provided is essentially a portion of the HYDRA manual’s table of contents, covering three consecutive chapters (3–5) and detailing the available commands (input), the structure of the output reports, and the options for graphical presentation of transient results.  It is arranged in three main blocks—Input Description (3.x), Output Description (4.x), and Graphical Output of Transient Results (5.x)—each subdivided into numbered entries.  Here is a breakdown of its structure and contents:

1. General Layout  
   • Three columns per row:  
     1. Section or command identifier (e.g. “3.7”, “4.1”, “5.1”)  
     2. Name or brief description of the command/section  
     3. Page reference in the manual (e.g. “3-10”, “4-1”, “5-1”)  
   • Main headings appear in bold (Input Description, Output Description, Graphical Output of Transient Results).  
   • Nested sub-sections illustrated by decimals (e.g. 3.10.1, 3.10.2, 3.10.3 under HMAT).

2. Input Description (Chapter 3)  
   Covers commands used to build, modify, and manage the finite‐element model before solving seepage or thermal problems. Entries include:  
   • 3.7 COPY – Modification of Results (p. 3-10)  
   • 3.8 GRP – Selection of Groups (p. 3-11)  
   • 3.9 NVAL – Material Values at Nodes (p. 3-13)  
   • 3.10 HMAT – Material Constants (HYDRA) (p. 3-14)  
       – 3.10.1 Hydraulic Parameters (p. 3-15)  
       – 3.10.2 Heat Conduction (p. 3-15)  
       – 3.10.3 Hydration of Concrete (p. 3-18)  
   • 3.11 LINK – Connecting Element (p. 3-20)  
   • 3.12 PIPE – Pipe or Channel Elements (p. 3-22)  
   • 3.13 LC – Analysis Case (p. 3-23)  
   • 3.14 BOUN – Boundary Conditions (p. 3-24)  
       – 3.14.1 Thermal Conductivity and Emissivity (p. 3-26)  
   • 3.15 SURF – Surface and Volume Boundary Conditions (p. 3-28)  
   • 3.16 FUNC – Transient Conditions (p. 3-30)  
   • 3.17 HIST – Transient Results (p. 3-32)  
   • 3.18 COPY – Modify Nodal Results in the Database (p. 3-33)  
   • 3.19 IMPO – Import of Results (p. 3-34)  
   • 3.20 ECHO – Output Options (p. 3-35)  

3. Output Description (Chapter 4)  
   Lists the various parts of the printed or file-based report that HYDRA generates once the analysis is complete. Each sub-section points to the page where the report format and content are defined:  
   • 4.1 System Parameters (p. 4-1)  
   • 4.2 Nodes (p. 4-1)  
   • 4.3 Materials (p. 4-1)  
   • 4.4 Sections (p. 4-2)  
   • 4.5 Elements (p. 4-2)  
   • 4.6 Boundary Conditions (p. 4-3)  
   • 4.7 Statistical Information (p. 4-4)  
   • 4.8 Results of the Elements (p. 4-4)  
   • 4.9 Results at Nodes (p. 4-5)  
   • 4.10 Balancing (p. 4-5)  

4. Graphical Output of Transient Results (Chapter 5)  
   Focuses on the commands that control graphics settings for plotting time-dependent data:  
   • 5.1 SIZE – Graphic Format (p. 5-1)  
   • 5.2 SCHH – Set Character Heights (p. 5-2)  
   • 5.3 FUNC – External Function (p. 5-3)  

Key observations for RAG integration:  
• The table entries map command keywords to their descriptive purpose and the exact manual page where they are documented.  
• Hierarchical numbering reflects logical grouping (e.g. HMAT’s three physical‐property sub-commands).  
• Consistent formatting makes it straightforward to index commands, their functions, and references.  
• This structure can be converted into a knowledge base where each command node links to its definition, input parameters, and related output sections.

 A great number of physical problems may be described as potential problems governed by the Laplace (ΔH = 0) or the Poisson differential equation (ΔH = q). Among these are magnetic flow, heatflow and groundwater seepage. HYDRA is specialised on the the last and last but one type of problem, but may be used for other problems with a similar background as well.
 A finite element method discretizes the real continua in a finite number of small elements with simplified physical properties. The elements are connected at nodes. An interpolation function within the elements represents a numerical estimate to the real solution.
 Thermal analysis allows the evaluation of the temperature distribution within a solid due to a steady or transient heating or cooling or temperature gradient.
 Groundwater models are used to compute the movement of water (seepage) within a porous solid needed for geology, hydrology, soil mechanics or groundwater supply.
 Problems of seepage may be subdivided in categories, matching different requests of preci- sion.
 • Plane or 3D problems
 The real situation is always 3D. For the analysis you may select a system which ne- glects one of the dimensions. For a structure extending along a line like a dam, we may select a plane cut with constant thickness. For aquifers with a vertical thickness much less than the horizontal dimensions, we may use the hypothesis of Dupuit to switch to a simplified, but not necessarily plane system.
 • Linear or nonlinear flow models
 Nonlinear flow is needed for turbulent flow, this is important for pipes and culverts but not so for seepage. However one important case is the free surface problem. All nonlinear problems may be solved with an iterative procedure.
 • Free, confined or partial saturated flow
 The free surface problem is governed by a surface with pressure zero, which is the boundary of the flow domain and is not known a priori. A partial saturated flow may be accounted for with a pressure dependant conductivity to some extend.

The figure is a temperature–time heat-evolution plot for hydrating concrete, showing calculated and experimental curves of the cumulative heat release Q(t) (in joules per gram) as a function of the actual concrete age t (in days). Key features are:

1. Axes and grid  
   • Vertical axis: “Wärmemenge Q(t) [J/g]” from 0 up to 300 J/g, with major grid lines every 50 J/g.  
   • Horizontal axis: “tatsächliches Betonalter [d]” from 0 to 96 days, with major grid lines every 12 days (0, 12, 24, …, 96).

2. Annotated fit parameters (upper-left corner)  
   • tₖ = 146.279 (a characteristic time constant, in days)  
   • a = –0.95 (dimensionless exponent)  
   • b = 0.137 (rate parameter)  
   • c = 313 (asymptotic heat release, J/g)

3. Analytical function (upper-right overlay)  
   Just to the right of the parameter box a semi-transparent formula is printed in light grey:  
     313 ⋆ e^(–0.137 ⋅ (ln(1 + x / 146))^–0.…  
   This expresses the curve of ultimate (adiabatic) heat release as a decaying exponential in the transformed time variable ln(1 + t/tₖ).

4. Four curves in the main plotting area  
   a) Long-dashed line (“adiabatisch”):  
      – This theoretical adiabatic model curve starts at Q(0)=0, rises steeply during the first few days, and then asymptotically approaches Q ≃ 313 J/g by roughly 80–90 days. It represents the maximum possible heat release if the concrete were perfectly insulated (no heat loss).  
   b) Solid line (“isotherm”):  
      – Rising more slowly than the adiabatic curve, it reaches about 150 J/g by day 10 and then continues gradually upward, leveling out near 250 J/g by day 90. This is the heat release under an assumed constant temperature regime (“isothermal” condition).  
   c) Thick dashed-and-dotted line (labelled “Jonas” or experimental Jonas data):  
      – Exhibits a pronounced peak of ~160 J/g around day 8–10, followed by a rapid decline to ~20 J/g by day 40, and then tails off slowly toward zero additional release. This suggests a core-shrinkage or laboratory batch test where cumulative heat release slows sharply after an early hydration surge.  
   d) Thin dotted line (second “Jonas” variant, sometimes referred to as a corrected or alternative Jonas fit):  
      – Sits between the isothermal and pure experimental Jonas curves, rising to roughly 220 J/g by day 50 and then plateauing near 240 J/g. It appears to be an adjusted model curve that fits the experimental datapoints more closely at intermediate ages.

5. Legend and line-style keys  
   • “adiabatisch” long dashes  
   • “isotherm” solid  
   • “Jonas” thick dash-dot  
   • “Jonas” (alternative fit) fine dots  

6. Interpretation in context of heat-conduction modeling  
   – If one inserts the classical Fourier heat-conduction law ∂Q/∂t = ∇⋅(λ∇T) into the local energy balance ρ cₚ ∂T/∂t = −∂Q/∂t (or, with ρ cₚ combined into a storage coefficient S), one obtains a governing differential equation whose solution must match one of these empirical curves.  
   – Of the two control-temperature efficiency definitions (CTRL TEFF 1 by Saul’s enhancement for –10 °C<T<+50 °C versus CTRL TEFF 2 by Freiesleben for –10 °C<T<80 °C), the Freiesleben definition generally gives the best match to the adiabatic asymptote (c=313 J/g) and is thus recommended as the default.  
   – The “Shrinkage-Core” model (b = fcc(28 d) ≈ 0.55 ⋅ exp(c ⋅ t)) is another alternative but not explicitly plotted here.

Overall, Figure 2.1 provides a comprehensive comparison between:

   – a smoothed Jonas fit that bridges theory and measurement. This multi-curve representation underpins selection of model parameters (tₖ, a, b, c) and the proper definition of “effective temperature” for numerical simulation of thermal behavior in hardening concrete.

In hydraulics it is common to express the energy of the fluid via the elevation of the fluid above a reference level (piezometric head or potential) which is called h and composed of:
 - geodetic height (potential energy) z - pressure heigth p/γ - velocity height v2/2g - stream height (acceleration energy)
 ”Integral”
 For groundwater seepage the velocities are small enough to allow to neglect the last two terms.
 For the coordinate z you may use any other coordinate axis with a positive or negative sign.
 A movement of the groundwater will always occur from the higher value of the potential to the lower through a connecting material with hydraulic conductivity.
 If the soil does not only contain water but also air, one has a so-called multiphase flow which cannot be used in HYDRA in the form of coupled differential equations. However, there are possibilities for the description of partial saturated flows. One can introduce itself very well the negative suctions as the height of capillary rise. A sufficient fine-grained soil may move upward with its capillary water. Thus it has in the dry state a suction which corresponds to this maximum height of capillary rise.
 In the area of the saturated pore volume the pressure increases linearly with the depth, so that the piezometric height and the position height are added to a constant value. It is very important, that a constant pressure has to be available in all points above the capillary line. It results consequently from top to bottom a gradient of the potential, which corresponds to the geodetic height. The gradient is therefore 1.0.

The figure is a schematic plot of how the “effective” hydraulic conductivity (denoted K or k on the vertical axis) depends on the hydraulic gradient i = ∂h/∂x (horizontal axis).  It is laid out on a lightly gridded background, with both axes drawn as bold lines ending in arrowheads (vertical arrow to indicate increasing K or k; horizontal arrow for increasing i).  Across the top of the diagram three flow‐regimes are named, separated by two vertical dashed guide‐lines:

 1.  “no flow” (far left)  
 2.  “plastic” (middle)  
 3.  “linear” (right)  

On the horizontal axis, at the very bottom, the gradient i is explicitly defined as i = ∂h/∂x and three special gradient values are marked beneath the axis:

 •  i₍I,II₎ (the first threshold) aligns with the left dashed line  
 •  i₍II,III₎ (the second threshold) aligns with the right dashed line  
 •  i₍III,IV₎  (if shown) would lie further to the right, beyond the plotted region  

The vertical dashed lines at i₍I,II₎ and i₍II,III₎ partition the plot into the three regimes mentioned above.

Within the “no flow” zone (i < i₍I,II₎), the bold curve sits on the horizontal axis at zero conductivity, indicating that until the hydraulic gradient reaches the first critical value, no measurable Darcy‐type flow takes place.  As soon as the gradient exceeds i₍I,II₎ the system enters the “plastic” regime: here the graph shows a smooth, upward‐curving S‐shape.  In this middle region, K (or k) increases nonlinearly with i, first slowly (concave up), then more steeply through an inflection, and finally tapering off (concave down) as the gradient approaches the next critical value i₍II,III₎.

Once i surpasses the second threshold i₍II,III₎, the curve flattens out into a nearly horizontal line in the “linear” regime.  This plateau indicates that for large gradients, the medium behaves according to Darcy’s law with a constant conductivity tensor K – the point at which v = –K·grad H becomes a strictly linear relationship again.

At the bottom right corner of the figure is the caption “Figure 2.2.”  Overall, the diagram offers a visual summary of a three‐stage response of hydraulic conductivity to increasing hydraulic gradient: zero flow up to a first yield threshold, a plastic (non‐linear, strain‐hardening‐like) transition, and finally a return to linear Darcy flow at high gradients.  It neatly illustrates why, in numerical modeling of groundwater movement, heterogeneous permeabilities and nonlinear flow laws can pose both conceptual and computational challenges.

The image is a schematic, cross-sectional sketch labeled “Figure 2.3: Dupuit-Hypothesis,” intended to illustrate how, under the Dupuit assumption, a three-dimensional groundwater flow problem collapses into two dimensions when the horizontal extent of an aquifer greatly exceeds its vertical thickness.  The drawing can be described as follows:

1. Overall Geometry  
   - Two nearly vertical lines mark the top and bottom boundaries of a thin, horizontally expansive porous stratum (a confined aquifer layer).  
   - The upper boundary is drawn as a nearly horizontal line, representing either the impermeable cap or ground surface (depending on context).  
   - The lower boundary is depicted as a straight horizontal baseline, representing the base of the aquifer (another impermeable or low-permeability horizon).

2. Real vs. Assumed Piezometric Head  
   - Between these two boundaries, on the left half of the sketch, a gently curved line arcs from the top boundary down toward the base. This curved profile is labeled “real Piezometric head,” indicating that, in reality, the hydraulic head varies slightly with depth within the stratum.  
   - On the right half, instead of a curve, a single straight vertical line is drawn within the thickness of the layer and labeled “assumed Piezometric head.” This vertical line signifies the Dupuit hypothesis: the hydraulic head is taken as constant across the entire thickness of the saturated zone at any given horizontal location.

3. Implication of the Dupuit Approximation  
   - By replacing the actual, depth-varying head with a constant value across the layer’s thickness, the flow problem is reduced from fully three-dimensional to an effective two-dimensional one (plan view plus one vertical coordinate collapsed).  
   - In practical terms, the aquifer’s hydraulic conductivity tensor across its thickness is integrated to yield a single transmissivity parameter T, simplifying calculations of horizontal flow.

4. Visual Emphasis and Labeling  
   - The contrast between the curved “real” line and the straight “assumed” line drives home the central idea: small vertical head differences are neglected.  
   - Both labels are positioned just outside the layer, with arrowheads pointing to their respective lines.  
   - A concise caption beneath the drawing (“Figure 2.3: Dupuit-Hypothesis”) anchors the sketch within the text.

In summary, this figure visually encapsulates the key assumption of the Dupuit hypothesis: that within a thin, laterally extensive aquifer, vertical head variations can be ignored, enabling the use of transmissivity in place of full conductivity profiling and thereby reducing a complex 3D flow problem to a manageable 2D formulation.

The provided sketch (Figure 2.4) is a schematic cross-section of an unconfined groundwater flow domain, showing the principal boundary segments and the characteristic families of lines (equipotentials and streamlines) that define the flow field. Below is a detailed, structured description of what is depicted:

1. Overall Geometry  
   • The solid black outline traces the shape of an idealized dam or embankment sitting on an impermeable foundation.  
   • The left flank slopes up from the foundation to a flat crest; the right flank slopes down.  
   • The foundation at the bottom is assumed impermeable (no flow across it).

2. Upstream Water Level (Dirichlet Boundary)  
   • At the very top of the left side, a short horizontal line marked “H0” denotes the prescribed piezometric head (the constant hydraulic potential) of the reservoir impounded behind the dam.  
   • A downward-pointing triangular “pointer” symbol just beneath that line reinforces that this is a fixed head boundary (Dirichlet condition) where H = H0.

3. Potential Line (Equipotential)  
   • Beginning at the reservoir level H0, a gently curving line labeled “Potential line” follows the sloping upstream face of the embankment and meets the free surface at a single point.  
   • Along this boundary, the total piezometric head remains constant (H = H0) in accordance with equation (2.49).  
   • No hydraulic gradient is tangential to this curve; it is an equipotential boundary.

4. Free Surface (Unknown Boundary)  
   • The curve labeled “Free Surface” arcs from the meeting point on the upstream slope, passes through the interior of the dam body, and emerges on the downstream face, falling toward the toe.  
   • This boundary represents the phreatic (water table) surface, where the fluid pressure equals atmospheric pressure (p = 0). Its exact shape is not known in advance and must be located iteratively in a seepage analysis.  
   • The free surface carries a Neumann-type condition (natural boundary) in which the normal derivative of head corresponds to zero pressure difference relative to atmosphere.

5. Flow Lines (Streamlines or Flux Lines)  
   • A family of almost vertical, slightly fanning lines drawn between the potential line (or crest) and the impermeable foundation/toe represents streamlines of equal discharge (Q = Q0), each satisfying the condition q·n = 0 on impermeable boundaries.  
   • These lines originate from the equipotential on the left and terminate at the downstream toe, illustrating how water flows through the porous medium.  
   • They are orthogonal to the equipotential (potential) lines at every intersection, reflecting Darcy’s law directionality.

6. Impermeable Boundaries (Neumann Condition)  
   • The bottom foundation is shown by a straight line labeled implicitly as “flow line” in the figure text – in reality it is an impermeable boundary: no normal flow, q·n = 0 (equation 2.51).  
   • Similarly, any portion of the embankment surfaces not occupied by the reservoir head or the free surface is also impermeable.  

7. Annotation and Labeling  
   • “Flow line” is written along the base to indicate the set of streamlines that would coincide with that boundary if extended.  
   • The caption reads “Figure 2.4: Boundary conditions of unconfined flow,” situating this schematic within a broader discussion of Darcy-type boundary conditions: Dirichlet (fixed head), Neumann (specified flux or impermeable), and the natural (free) surface.  
   • No dimensions or numeric scales are given; the drawing is purely conceptual.

8. Interpretive Context  
   • The image visually summarizes how:  
     – A known upstream head H0 is imposed (Dirichlet).  
     – The phreatic surface must emerge from the geometry under zero‐pressure conditions.  
     – The base and any dry parts of the surface impose zero normal flux (impermeable).  
     – Flow lines fill the interior and demonstrate the pattern of groundwater movement.  
   • In practical seepage analyses, the free surface location and any intersection points with the embankment must be found iteratively because of their dependence on the internal flow field.

3.  Record EPS  (Element Property Set)  
   Purpose: define cross‐sectional or material properties for a group of elements.  
   Fields:  
     1) EPSID (I) – unique element‐property identifier.  
     2) ETYPE (C) – element type code (e.g. “PLATE”, “BEAM”).  
     3) MAT   (I) – material number reference.  
     4) THK   (R) – thickness (only for shell‐type elements).

     2) ELM  (I) – beam element number.  
     3) LOC  (R) – normalized location along the beam (0…1).

     – REST: “REUse exiSTing main system.”  No new mesh or system directory look-up is done.  
     – SECT: Pull in the pre‐computed FEM mesh for a specific cross‐section (see SNO).  If the section mesh does not yet exist, HYDRA can generate a simple rectangular T‐beam or circular/annular mesh on the fly (provided CTRL STYP FEMX was set before).  
   • When TYPE=SECT, the SNO field below becomes mandatory.  Otherwise SNO is ignored.

3. Field “SNO” (integer, no default)  
   • Section Number.  Identifies which pre‐meshed section’s FE‐subsystem to load.  
   • Must correspond to a subdirectory under the global “FE‐Systems” directory tree, created by AQUA under CTRL STYP FEMX or by a previous run.  
   • No unit or default because it is only relevant for TYPE=SECT.

4. Field “GDIR” (literal, default = NEGZ)  
   • Gravity direction for seepage and structural‐weight analyses.  Always a single axis label.  
   • Positive‐axis options: POSX, POSY, POSZ  
   • Negative‐axis options: NEGX, NEGY, NEGZ  
   • Defaults to NEGZ (i.e. gravity acting in the negative global‐Z).  
   • Influences body‐force vectors and hydrostatic boundary conditions when you define fluid loads via STEP or GRP.

5. Field “DIMT” (literal, default = SEC)  
   • Unit of time for all input time‐functions, step lengths, and time‐based output quantities.  
   • Valid codes:  
     – SEC for seconds  
     – MIN for minutes  
     – H   for hours  
     – D   for days  
   • Changing DIMT has a wide effect: it rescales any time‐dependent boundary curves defined in STEP, any transient solver time steps, and any output tables that carry a time column.

6. Field “DIMQ” (literal, default = L)  
   • Unit system for all scalar and vector fields (pressures, volumes, fluxes, temperatures, power, diffusion rates) in both input BCs and output results.  
   • Valid codes and their interpretations:  
     – KG   → activates vapour‐diffusion mode (mass‐flux basis; often interpreted as kg/m²·s)  
     – L    → liter (for volumetric tasks or simple storage problems)  
     – M3   → cubic meter (structural volumes, large‐scale hydrology)  
     – W    → Watt·DIMT, temperatures in Celsius (standard heat‐flow problem)  
     – KW   → Kilowatt·DIMT, °C  
     – MW   → Megawatt·DIMT, °C  
     – AW   → Watt·DIMT, temperatures in Kelvin (absolute‐T formulation)  
     – AKW  → Kilowatt·DIMT, Kelvin  
     – AMW  → Megawatt·DIMT, Kelvin  
   • The choice of W/KW/MW vs. AW/AKW/AMW also toggles whether you solve in °C or in absolute Kelvin.  
   • Note: KG is _only_ valid when you intend a vapour‐diffusion analysis, _not_ a thermal run.

Summary of defaults and interplay:  
• Unless you explicitly override, HYDRA will: TYPE=REST (reuse main system), GDIR=NEGZ, DIMT=SEC, DIMQ=L, and ignore SNO.  
• To spin up a new section mesh and run a thermal transient in kilowatts and minutes, you’d do for example:  
   SYST TYPE=SECT SNO=102 GDIR=POSY DIMT=MIN DIMQ=KW  
• Always precede SYST by any CTRL settings (CTRL HDIV, CTRL STYP FEMX) needed to ensure the mesh exists or is generated correctly.

The table defines a simple four-column schema for specifying control parameters (“options”) in a flow/transport simulation module.  It is intended to be parsed into a Retrieval‐Augmented Generation (RAG) vector store so that each option (and its numeric settings) can be retrieved, indexed, and related to its meaning, units and defaults.  Below is a breakdown of the table’s structure, its record types, and how it ties together with the contextual notes.

1. Overall Structure  
   • Columns  
     – Item: a short code indicating the type of record or the option name.  
     – Description: textual explanation of what the code or value means.  
     – Unit: the physical (or syntactic) unit associated with the field.  
     – Default: the fallback value if none is provided.  

   • Four “Item” record types  
     – OPT: declares the **option names** (literal strings) and lists all recognized option codes.  
     – VAL: carries the **primary numeric value** for a given option.  
     – V2: carries the **secondary numeric value** for those options that accept two numbers.  
     – V3: carries the **tertiary numeric value** for those options that need three.  

2. OPT Record (Item = “OPT”)  
   • Unit = LIT (literal string)  
   • Default = “–” (no default; user must supply one of the listed codes)  
   • Description header: “Designation of an Option”  
   • Sub-entries (each is a valid option code + brief meaning):  
     AFIX   — Treatment of multivalued systems  
     SCON   — Type of capacity matrix  
     FROB   — Free-surface/unconfined flow (0=no; 1=account; 2=incl. velocity head)  
     TURB   — Turbulent flow model  
     SOLV   — Equation solver (3=serial; 4=PARDISO parallel)  
     KITE   — Iteration method  
     GEN    — Precision of iteration  
     MITE   — Maximum number of iterations  
     ETOL   — Tolerance of line-search  
     HDIF   — Allowed change of potential  
     FMAX   — Maximum acceleration factor for extrapolation  
     FMUL   — Maximum increase factor (damping control)  
     LDIF   — Store difference values at current loop + LDIF flag  
     HLIM   — Break-off limit for potential change  
     VLIM   — Break-off limit for flux change  
     GAM    — Specific weight of flow media (units kN/m³)  
     KZ     — Kinematic viscosity (units sec/cm², for pipe elements)  
     TEFF   — Effective age of concrete (various empirical definitions)  
     HDIV   — Mesh‐density control for finite‐element cross-sections  

3. VAL / V2 / V3 Records  
   • Units = “*” (wildcard, numeric)  
   • Defaults: VAL = “!” (mandatory), V2 = “–”, V3 = “–”  
   • Description fields:  
     – VAL: “Value of the Option” (the first or only numeric parameter)  
     – V2: “second value for some options”  
     – V3: “third value for some options”  

   In practice this allows, for instance:  
     • For SOLV you supply VAL=3 to choose the serial solver or VAL=4 for PARDISO.  
     • For FROB you could set VAL=2 if you need to include velocity head.  
     • For GAM and KZ you enter the specific weight or kinematic viscosity in VAL.  
     • If an option like TEFF needs two coefficients (e.g., Saul’s A0/A1), VAL and V2 can hold them.  

4. Contextual Notes (from the additional text)  
   • Several iteration solvers benefit from tangent‐stiffness or quasi‐Newton methods,  
     especially under free-surface flow where boundary conditions frequently change.  
   • Damping and extrapolation controls (FMAX <1 for damping, FMUL=0 to disable growth)  
     help stabilize and speed up convergence.  
   • Break-off tolerances HLIM and VLIM trigger an immediate halt if successive iterations  
     differ by more than HTOL (potential) or VTOL (flux) relative to the base state.  
   • TEFF uses one of four empirical definitions (Saul, Freiesleben, Jonasson, etc.),  
     selected by VAL=0..3 with optional V2/V3 coefficients.  

5. How this maps into a RAG Vector Store  
   • Each OPT entry becomes a document embedding keyed by the option code (e.g. “SOLV”)  
     and carries metadata = { description, unit, default }.  
   • VAL/V2/V3 documents link back via foreign key (option code) and store the numeric payloads.  
   • Additional narrative from the “Remarks” section is attached as auxiliary metadata  
     to options like KITE, HDIF, FMAX, FMUL, HLIM, VLIM, TEFF.  

By indexing the table in this way—splitting literal option definitions from their numeric values and capturing unit/default information—you enable precise, context-aware retrieval of both “Which option do I use to set the solver?” and “What numeric arguments does it expect?”

The table summarizes the six key input parameters that govern how a transient (time-dependent) analysis is carried out. Together, they let you choose between a fixed time step, a geometrically-growing set of steps, or an adaptive scheme that automatically adjusts step size to control how quickly the solution (“potential”) changes. Below is a detailed breakdown of each row:

1. N (Number of time steps)  
   • Description: Determines how many individual time increments the solver will execute.  
   • How it’s used:  
     – If N > 1, the solver treats N as the exact count of steps. The total simulated time will be the sum of all those steps.  
     – If N < 1 (for instance 0.001), then N becomes the fraction of the total time T that defines the first step. Subsequent steps follow the progression rules below.  
   • Unit: dimensionless  
   • Default: 0   (which effectively defers to the rule for N < 1, making the first step a fraction of T)

2. T (Time value of first step or total Time)  
   • Description: Depending on N, this can mean either the duration of the very first time step or the overall simulation time.  
   • How it’s used:  
     – If N > 1, T is the duration of the initial step; all subsequent steps are then generated by multiplication with TFAK or by the adaptive algorithm.  
     – If N < 1, T is interpreted directly as the total time span to be covered.  
   • Unit: DIMT (an internal time unit specific to the solver)  
   • Default: 1

3. TFAK (Factor for time steps)  
   • Description: The multiplier used to grow (or shrink) each new time step relative to the previous one.  
   • Two primary roles:  
     – Geometric progression: stepₙ₊₁ = stepₙ × TFAK.  
     – Automatic mode: TFAK sets how aggressively the solver will expand or contract a time step around the “optimal” step size HOPT, using the thresholds TFAC·HOPT and HOPT/TFAC.  
   • Unit: dimensionless  
   • Default: 1

4. THET (Coefficient of time integration)  
   • Description: A weighting factor in the time-integration scheme (often used in Θ-methods that blend explicit and implicit approaches).  
   • Range: 0.5 ≤ Θ < 2.0  
   • Effect:  
     – Θ = 0.5 corresponds to the Crank–Nicolson method (second-order accurate, unconditionally stable).  
     – Θ = 1.0 is fully implicit (first-order accurate, very stable).  
     – Values above 1.0 introduce numerical damping.  
   • Unit: dimensionless  
   • Default: 0.7

5. HOPT (Optimal change of potential)  
   • Description: A target threshold for how much the solution (e.g., electrical potential) is allowed to change per time step. It guides the automatic step-size controller.  
   • Role in automatic mode:  
     – If the actual change exceeds TFAK × HOPT, the solver reduces the time step and retries.  
     – If the actual change is below HOPT / TFAK, the next time step is enlarged by factor TFAK.  
   • Unit: m/K (meters per Kelvin, or the unit in which “potential change” is measured)  
   • Default: (no fixed default; user must supply a meaningful value)

6. TMIN (Smallest allowed time step for HOPT)  
   • Description: A lower bound on how small any time step can be when the automatic controller reduces step size in order to meet the HOPT criterion.  
   • Unit: DIMT  
   • Default: 0.001 T  (i.e., one-thousandth of the total time value T)

In practice, you start by choosing whether you need a fixed stepping scheme (set N > 1, T and TFAK to constants) or an adaptive scheme (provide HOPT, let TFAC default to 1.4 if not specified). You then refine THET based on your desired stability and accuracy. Finally, TMIN prevents runaway reductions in step size. Together, these parameters offer a flexible framework that can handle simple constant-step runs, fast geometric sequences, or robust, error-controlled transient simulations.

See also: CTRL

 The size of the (n+1)th time step is established by multiplication of the nth time step with TFAC. For larger numbers of time steps it is advisable to check the given values with a pocket calculator, as the time steps can grow rather high if TFAC is chosen improper.

Whenever the change of the potential exceeds TFAC·HOPT, the time step will be reduced and the step repeated. Is the change however less than HOPT/TFAC, the next time step will be enlarged by factor TFAC.

Below is a structured, detailed description of each input-table entry in the context of PLC transient (and deviation) analyses.  These parameters define the “primary estate” (i.e. the driving potential field and its initialization) for flow or consolidation simulations, support correct time-interpolation of results, and enable special operations such as copying or combining load cases.

1. Overview  
   • Each record begins with an item code (NO, T, HP, etc.), followed by a text description, its physical unit, and the default value if the user does not supply one.  
   • Collectively they set up initial and boundary values for potentials (e.g. pore pressure or hydraulic head), specify gradients, and control time-stepping behavior.  
   • Special keywords (e.g. literal CONT for T) and auxiliary commands (e.g. COPY, GRP, HMAT) allow advanced manipulations.

2. Item-by-Item Breakdown

  NO  
   • “Number of primary load case.”  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: none (user must assign).  
   • Use: Identifies the reference load case (estate) from which transient analysis or a deviation run starts.  NO ties this input line to a stored result set.

  T  
   • “Time value at start of this analysis.”  
   • Unit: DIMT (time dimension).  
   • Default: last stored time (denoted “*”).  
   • Use: Specifies the time stamp for interpolation of prior results and for graphics.  If set to the literal CONT, all potential values (even from earlier steps) are re-copied into the current case—a convenience for postprocessing but incompatible with element-based result updates.

  HP  
   • “Constant value of primary potential.”  
   • Unit: morK (model-specific head/pressure unit).  
   • Default: 0.  
   • Use: Applies a uniform baseline potential to all nodes.  Can be overridden or augmented by group-level values (via GRP) or by the spatial gradients below.

  DHPX, DHPY, DHPZ  
   • “Global gradient of primary estate along X, Y, Z.”  
   • Units: m/m (or K/m).  
   • Defaults: 0, 0, 0 respectively.  
   • Use: Introduces a linear variation: at any node with coordinates (X,Y,Z), the primary potential becomes  
       HP’ = HP + DHPX·X + DHPY·Y + DHPZ·Z.  
     This allows sloping water-table or hydrostatic head distributions.

  DHTF  
   • “Factor for time derivatives.”  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: 0.0.  
   • Use: If set to 1.0, the code computes an initial time-derivative term from the last two stored estate values (difference divided by Δt).  This can improve convergence when boundary conditions change significantly at startup.  Otherwise, time derivatives are ignored.

  PU  
   • “Minimum pore water pressure for transition to free surface flow.”  
   • Unit: m  
   • Default: –9999.0  
   • Use: Acts as a lower clamp on pore pressure.  Nodes where computed pressure would drop below this threshold are treated as having a free surface.

  LCS  
   • “Structural load case for stresses.”  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: none.  
   • Use: Specifies an external structural analysis case whose stress field modifies flow transmissivities via user-defined relations (HMAT FVOL/FSIG).

  LCU, LCU0  
   • “Structural load cases for pore water pressures derived from LCU–LCU0.”  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: none.  
   • Use: Together these designate two structural cases whose differential volumetric stress (Δσx+Δσy+Δσz)/3 is converted into an initial pore pressure for a consolidation run via  
       H = h – (1/3·Δσsum)/γ.  

3. Related Utilities  
   • GROUP (GRP): assign primary potentials to node groups; nodes in multiple groups inherit the mean.  
   • COPY: combine or shift/scale pressure fields across transient results.  

By setting these parameters thoughtfully, you can initialize complex spatial distributions, enforce physical bounds, link structural-hydraulic couplings, and streamline graphical post-processing in RAG-based vector stores.

The table in question defines five configuration items used to generate or transform load‐case numbers and to apply simple arithmetic corrections to pressure values. It is organized into four columns—Item, Description, Unit, and Default—and five rows, one for each configurable parameter. Below is a structured breakdown of its contents and intended meaning.

1. Column Headings  
   • Item  
     – The short code or keyword used in an input file, script, or GUI field.  
   • Description  
     – A concise narrative explaining the purpose and effect of the parameter.  
   • Unit  
     – Indicates whether the parameter is dimensionless or carries a unit symbol. An asterisk (*) denotes a multiplier or divisor, while a dash (–) means “not applicable” or “no units.”  
   • Default  
     – The value assumed if the user does not explicitly supply one. Default values may refer to other items by name.

2. Row-by-Row Explanation  
   a) FROM  
      • Description: “First number of a primary load case.”  
      • Unit: – (unitless).  
      • Default: “–” (no default; this value must be provided by the user).  
      • Purpose: Specifies the starting index or identifier for a sequence of primary load cases. For example, if you wish to process load cases 10 through 20, you would set FROM = 10.  
   b) TO  
      • Description: “Last number of a primary load case.”  
      • Unit: – (unitless).  
      • Default: FROM (automatically uses the FROM value if not explicitly set).  
      • Purpose: Defines the ending index in the same sequence. By defaulting to FROM, the system handles single‐case scenarios without additional input. If FROM = 10 and TO is omitted, TO defaults to 10.  
   c) TARG  
      • Description: “Resulting load case number.”  
      • Unit: – (unitless).  
      • Default: FROM.  
      • Purpose: Indicates the target or output load case number for the result of any merging, summation, or remapping operation. If not specified, the processed load case(es) will be written back under the same number as the first input (FROM).  
   d) PCOR  
      • Description: “Shift of pressure values by.”  
      • Unit: * (multiplier for pressure data).  
      • Default: 0.0.  
      • Purpose: Applies an additive constant to all pressure readings in the specified load case range. A value of 0.0 means no shift. Positive values raise the entire pressure profile, while negative values lower it. Useful for zero‐offset correction or baseline adjustments.  
   e) PREF  
      • Description: “Divide pressure values by.”  
      • Unit: * (divisor for pressure data).  
      • Default: 1.0.  
      • Purpose: Scales all pressure readings in the chosen load cases by dividing them by the given factor. A default of 1.0 leaves data unchanged. Setting PREF to 2.0 halves every pressure value, which can be used for unit conversions or normalization.

3. Typical Usage Pattern  
   • A user first sets FROM (required) to specify the starting load case.  
   • Optionally, they set TO to create a range; otherwise TO = FROM.  
   • TARG designates where the processed results are stored; if omitted, it defaults to FROM.  
   • PCOR and PREF permit on‐the‐fly corrections: PCOR shifts the baseline, while PREF rescales the magnitude.  
   • All parameters are combined in a single directive or block to perform batch processing of load cases and associated pressure data.

4. Relevance for RAG Vector Store  
   • Each of these items, along with its description and default, becomes a document or embedding in the vector store.  
   • Queries like “How do I apply a pressure offset?” or “What’s the default target load case?” can retrieve the relevant row and explanation.  
   • The table structure ensures that both parameter names and their semantics are captured for retrieval‐augmented generation workflows.

The table shown defines the control parameters associated with a GRP (group) record in a HYDRA‐style boundary‐loading or free‐surface analysis.  Each row corresponds to one of six “Item” fields (NO, LEV, LOAD, HP, HC, TF), and the columns give a concise “Description,” its physical “Unit,” and the “Default” value if none is supplied.

1.  NO  (Group number)  
    •  Description: Identifies the group to which subsequent elements belong.  When the GRP record is read, each element in the input immediately following is tagged with its element number plus (group_number × group_divisor).  This allows selective activation or deactivation of parts of the mesh in later steps by using LEV=OFF or by specifying other group numbers.  
    •  Unit: Lit/– (integer literal)  
    •  Default: “*” (all groups)—if no group number is specified, the record applies to every element.

2.  LEV  (Level of usage)  
    •  Description: Governs whether this group is active and whether results are printed.  
       – OFF: do not use this group in the solution  
       – YES: include this group in the computation but suppress any ASCII or graphical printout for it  
       – FULL: include the group and generate all associated output  
    •  Unit: LIT (literal keyword)  
    •  Default: FULL

3.  LOAD  (Save loading in the database)  
    •  Description: Determines which type of loading—buoyancy, streaming pressure, or thermal—is stored in the database for subsequent coupling (e.g., for TALPA or ASE post-processors).  Available flags:  
       – NONE: do not save any loading  
       – LIFT: buoyant load only (P = +γ · ∇Z)  
       – STRE: streaming pressure only (P = –γ · ∇H)  
       – PRES: combined buoyancy + streaming (P = –γ · ∇(H – Z))  
       – TEMP: temperature‐difference loading (uniform ΔT across the group)  
       – ATEM: absolute temperature (T in Kelvin or degrees)  
    •  Unit: LIT  
    •  Default: NEIN (no storage)

4.  HP  (Primary-state hydraulic potential)  
    •  Description: Specifies the initial pore‐pressure or hydraulic head (in primary state) assigned to all elements in this group.  Used when setting up initial conditions (see PLC record for advanced control).  
    •  Unit: m|o (meters of fluid column or equivalent pressure unit)  
    •  Default: none (–)

5.  HC  (Capillary suction zone height)  
    •  Description: Defines the thickness (in meters) of the unsaturated “suction” region immediately above the free surface.  HYDRA uses HC to create a smooth transition in permeability between saturated and dry zones.  
    •  Unit: m  
    •  Default: 0 (no capillary zone)

6.  TF  (Dry‐region permeability reduction factor)  
    •  Description: Multiplier applied to the soil permeability in any “non‐active” region above the free surface (i.e., the dry zone).  A small TF ensures numerical stability by preventing zero conductivity in the mesh.  
    •  Unit: – (dimensionless)  
    •  Default: 0.001

Contextual notes:  
–  GRP records work in tandem with the global “SYST GDIV” divisor: element IDs can be compartmentalized into multiple groups for sequenced solution steps.  
–  The LOAD options connect directly to HYDRA’s internal computation of buoyancy and streaming pressure gradients (P = γ · ∇Z, P = –γ·∇H), as well as uniform temperature loading for heat‐coupled analyses.  
–  Non‐active flow regions (where LEV=OFF or above the free surface) retain a small TF‐scaled conductivity so that heat or fluid exchange does not numerically stagnate.  
–  The HC parameter smooths the interface between saturated (active) and unsaturated (dry) soil layers, allowing partial‐saturation models to remain stable.

The table shown is the definition of the NVAL record, which allows you to assign material‐property values directly at individual nodes (or to all nodes) when assembling a finite‐element or finite‐difference model.  These “node-based” values are then picked up by any connecting elements (e.g. flow or heat‐transport elements) and may override or supplement a global material table (such as HMAT).  Below is a field-by-field breakdown of the columns and an explanation of how each row is used.

1. Column Headings  
   • Item  
     – The keyword or tag that identifies each datum in the NVAL record.  
   • Description  
     – A brief textual explanation of what the Item represents.  
   • Unit  
     – The physical unit in which the value must be supplied. A “–” means unitless or not applicable; “LIT” denotes a literal or enumerated text string; “*” means “as required by the TYPE”; and “!” indicates that a value is mandatory.  
   • Default  
     – The default value assumed if the field is omitted or blank. A dash (“–”) means “no default; optional,” while “!” means no default and is required.

2. Row Descriptions  
   NO (Node Number)  
     – Description: Specifies the node at which the values apply.  
     – Unit: – (unitless)  
     – Default: ! (required)  
     – Remarks: Use NO=0 to indicate “apply to all nodes” (a global assignment).  

   TYPE (Property Type)  
     – Description: Identifies which material property you are prescribing. See HMAT for a complete list of allowed property codes.  
     – Unit: LIT (literal, e.g. K, KXYZ, S, NSP, COPY)  
     – Default: ! (required)  
     – Possible values:  
         • K    – Isotropic permeability (Darcy’s law) in m/s or isotropic thermal conductivity in W/(m·K).  
         • KXYZ – Anisotropic permeability tensor (m/s) or thermal conductivity tensor (W/(m·K)).  
         • S    – Specific storage (groundwater storage coefficient, 1/m) or specific heat capacity term (J/(m³·K)).  
         • NSP  – Effective (usable) porosity (dimensionless).  
         • COPY – Pull values from an existing database case; use VAL–VAL6 as multiplicative factors.

   VAL, VAL2, VAL3, VAL4, VAL5, VAL6  
     – Description: Numeric entries that supply the value(s) for the chosen TYPE. The number required depends on TYPE:  
         • For K or S or NSP, only VAL (first column) is used; VAL2–VAL6 are ignored.  
         • For KXYZ (anisotropic tensor), supply up to six independent components in the order: VAL=kxx, VAL2=kyy, VAL3=kzz, VAL4=kxy, VAL5=kxz, VAL6=kyz.  
     – Unit: * (see TYPE for units)  
     – Default: – (optional except where required by TYPE)  

   COPY (Reference Case)  
     – Description: Name or index of an existing model case in the database whose material values you wish to re-use.  
     – Unit: – (unitless literal identifying the case)  
     – Default: – (optional)  
     – When COPY is specified, the numeric VAL–VAL6 are interpreted as scaling factors applied to the corresponding property values in the reference case. This is especially useful after an inversion or parameter‐identification run: you can take the best‐fit parameters and scale them back into physical units without rebuilding the HMAT table by hand.

3. How NVAL Relates to HMAT  
   – The HMAT table typically holds material definitions by material code, applicable to large regions or volumes. NVAL provides a way to granularly override those definitions at the nodal level.  
   – If you omit NVAL for a node, the solver will fall back on the HMAT assignment for that element or region. If you include NVAL, then the local TYPE and VAL values take precedence for all connected elements.

4. Usage Notes  
   – Make sure that TYPE and the number of VAL entries are consistent:  
       • TYPE=K  or S or NSP  → supply only VAL.  
       • TYPE=KXYZ           → supply VAL through VAL6.  
   – If you want one node to inherit an entire material profile from a previous model run, use COPY plus the six VAL factors (often set to 1.0 if you want a direct copy).  
   – The nodal approach (via NVAL) is particularly powerful when material properties change spatially in a continuous fashion or when you need to impose local heterogeneities in permeability, storage, or porosity without editing the global HMAT.

By following this schema, you can flexibly control physical properties on a node-by-node basis, enabling detailed heterogeneity and facilitating workflows that span forward simulation and parameter estimation.

The “HMAT” table defines up to three distinct material‐property laws (diffusion, seepage and heat flow) for a given material and allows up to 15 property‐sets at different temperatures (°C) or pore pressures (kPa).  In a nonlinear analysis the solver linearly interpolates between adjacent sets; abrupt jumps (e.g. 10× changes in permeability K or storage S) may degrade convergence and should be smoothed by transition zones or finer tolerances.

Below is a field‐by‐field breakdown:

1. NO  
   • Material number (integer index).  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: must be specified (“!”)  

2. TYPE  
   • Material‐law identifier (literal code, up to 4 chars).  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: “FOUR”  
   • Allowed values and their meaning:  
     – DARC: Linear Darcy seepage  
     – FORC: Nonlinear Forchheimer seepage  
     – MISS: Nonlinear Missbach seepage  
     – FLOW: General diffusion (e.g. vapor transport)  
     – FOUR: Linear Fourier heat conduction  
     – JONA: Jonasson hydration model  
     – HSCM: Shrinkage‐Core hydration model  
     – WESC: Danish hydration model (Wesche)  

3. TEMP  
   • Temperature (°C) or pore‐pressure level (kPa).  
   • Unit: “*” (user‐defined scale).  
   • Default: 0  

4. Permeability / Conductivity parameters  
   • KXX, KYY, KZZ (principal isotropic or diagonal anisotropic terms)  
     – Unit: “*”  
     – Defaults: KXX=0; KYY=KXX; KZZ=KXX  
   • KXY, KXZ, KYZ (off‐diagonal anisotropic terms)  
     – Unit: “*”  
     – Defaults: 0 for each  

   • For nonlinear seepage laws (FORC, MISS):  
     – FORC uses parameters A,B stored in KZZ,KXY positions  
     – MISS uses parameters C,M in KXY,KXZ  

5. S  
   • Specific capacity or storage coefficient (e.g. m³/(m³·kPa)).  
   • Unit: “*”  
   • Default: 0  

6. NSP  
   • Effective porosity or moisture content (dimensionless fraction).  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: must be specified (“*”)  

7. Hydration‐model parameters (only for TYPE=JONA, HSCM, WESC)  
   • A: constant a (unitless); Default: user must set (“*”)  
   • B: constant b (unitless; JONA & WESC only); Default: “*”  
   • C: constant c (unitless; WESC only); Default: “*”  
   • QMAX: maximum heat release per volume (kJ/m³); Default: 0  
   • TK: reference time (h); Default: 15  

8. TITL  
   • Material designation (up to 32‐char string).  
   • Unit: Lit32  
   • Default: “–” (empty)  

Usage notes:  
- You may define multiple rows (up to 15) under one material number to capture behavior over temperature or saturation ranges.  
- In coupled simulations large discontinuities in K or S should be avoided. If unavoidable, introduce intermediate property sets or refine solver settings.  
- Hydration models (JONA, HSCM, WESC) require the A–C constants plus QMAX and TK to characterize the exothermic reaction kinetics.

The table summarizes typical ranges of saturated hydraulic conductivity (k) for seven soil classes. All k-values are given in metres per second [m/sec], in accordance with seepage options DARC, FORC and MISS in HYDRA. Positive k indicates permeability under saturated conditions; for unsaturated regions, negative pressures may apply and k may be interpolated or varied by porosity for free-surface problems.

1. Table structure  
   • Column 1 (“Type of soil”): Seven standard soil categories, ordered from coarsest (highest permeability) to finest (lowest permeability).  
   • Column 2 (“k [m/sec]”): The lower and upper bounds of hydraulic conductivity for each category.

2. Soil classes and conductivity ranges  
   1. Sandy gravel  
      • k ≈ 5·10⁻⁴ to 3·10⁻³ m/sec  
      • Extremely permeable; typical of coarse, well-sorted mixtures of sand and gravel.  
   2. Gravelly sand  
      • k ≈ 2·10⁻⁴ to 1·10⁻³ m/sec  
      • Very permeable; predominantly sand matrix with gravel inclusions.  
   3. Medium sand  
      • k ≈ 1·10⁻⁴ to 4·10⁻⁴ m/sec  
      • High permeability; uniform sand grains without significant fines.  
   4. Silty sand  
      • k ≈ 1·10⁻⁵ to 2·10⁻⁴ m/sec  
      • Intermediate permeability; sand with moderate silt content reducing flow.  
   5. Sandy silt  
      • k ≈ 1·10⁻⁶ to 5·10⁻⁵ m/sec  
      • Lower permeability; primarily silt with some sand, retaining more water.  
   6. Silty clay  
      • k ≈ 1·10⁻⁸ to 5·10⁻⁶ m/sec  
      • Very low permeability; fine particles and clay layers impede flow.  
   7. Clay  
      • k ≈ 1·10⁻⁸ m/sec (order of magnitude)  
      • Extremely low conductivity; plastic clays that virtually block seepage.

3. Context and usage in HYDRA  
   • Units conform to the Darcy-based seepage formulations; for general diffusion (potential theory) units would be sec/m.  
   • If the model requires anisotropic permeability, each soil class can be assigned directional conductivities KXX, KYY and KZZ in [m/sec] using the same ranges as a base. Variants FSIN and FSIT allow modification across or perpendicular to cracks under a prescribed linear stress field.  
   • Storage coefficient (S) is not included here but would be specified in [m³/m] when pairing with k for transient groundwater modeling.  
   • Temperature (TEMP) appears as pressure in [kPa] in HYDRA’s pore-pressure modules, though not directly tabulated here.  
   • These k-ranges serve as default engineering values; users may override them by defining material properties at the element level (material number >0) or at the node level (number = 0), or by interpolating between known lab or field data.

4. Practical implications  
   • Higher k values (coarser soils) yield rapid infiltration and low buildup of hydraulic head.  
   • Lower k values (finer soils) require fine mesh discretization and may produce steep pressure gradients.  
   • For free-surface seepage, effective porosity adjustments may be applied to account for unsaturated storage capacity.

Below is a narrative description of the four input parameters shown in your table.  These parameters feed into various hydration‐degree, maturity and heat‐release laws (Jonasson/Byfors, “shrinkage‐core,” Danish/Wesche, Saul‐maturity etc.) used in mass‐concrete thermal analyses.

1.  TEMP  
   • Parameter name: TEMP  
   • Meaning: Reference temperature for maturity and hydration‐reaction rate corrections  
   • Units: °C  
   • Default/example value: 10 °C  
   • Role in modeling:  
     – Many maturity functions (e.g. Saul’s law) and rate‐acceleration factors use a difference between actual concrete temperature and a reference temperature. TEMP establishes that baseline.  
     – In Arrhenius‐type or equivalent‐age formulations, the degree of reaction α, the effective age τeff, or shrinkage models often include a term (T–TEMP) or an exponential function of T–TEMP to account for thermal activation.

2.  QMAX  
   • Parameter name: QMAX  
   • Meaning: Maximum (total) heat release per unit volume of concrete  
   • Units: kJ/m3  
   • Default/example value: user‐supplied “!” (must be defined for each mix)  
   • Role in modeling:  
     – Defines the asymptotic ceiling of cumulative heat evolution as hydration goes to completion (α→1).  
     – Used to scale any non‐dimensional heat‐evolution or hydration‐degree curves so that the computed heat release in kJ/m3 corresponds to the real thermal output of the mix.  
     – Combined with rate functions (e.g. Byfors, Jonasson) to predict temperature rise in mass concrete.

3.  TK  
   • Parameter name: TK (often denoted τk)  
   • Meaning: Reference or “kick‐off” time at which significant hydration begins  
   • Units: hours (h)  
   • Default/example value: 15 h  
   • Role in modeling:  
     – Appears in multiple formulations for α(τ): for example the extended Byfors/Jonasson law, α=1–exp[–((τ–τk)/b)ᶜ] for τ>τk (zero beforehand), or linear‐asymptotic forms.  
     – Acts as a time‐shift: no appreciable heat release or degree‐of‐hydration growth is assumed for τ<τk, so the model enforces an induction period.  
     – In “shrinkage‐core” or “HSCM” models, τk marks the transition from dormant to accelerating period, affecting predicted autogenous shrinkage and internal self‐desiccation.

4.  S  
   • Parameter name: S  
   • Meaning: Exponent in Saul’s maturity function  
   • Units: dimensionless  
   • Default/example value: 1.00  
   • Role in modeling:  
     – Saul’s law for equivalent age often takes the form: τeq = ∫ exp[–Ea/RT] dt  or simplified A·(T–Tref)^S·t, with S controlling the sensitivity of maturity to temperature above the reference.  
     – An S of 1.0 corresponds to a linear dependency on (T–TEMP); higher values amplify the temperature influence, lower values reduce it.  
     – When the chosen hydration or strength‐gain model relies on an equivalent‐time concept, the exponent S lets you tune the model to match laboratory calorimetry or maturity‐curve data.

General notes / cross‐references:  
– All four parameters are essential inputs to any heat‐of‐hydration‐driven thermal analysis, especially for large/mass concrete elements where internal temperatures and gradients matter.  
– QMAX scales the total heat, TK establishes the end of the dormant period, TEMP sets the baseline for thermal activation, and S shapes the temperature sensitivity of the maturity/age function.  
– If you choose the Danish‐Wesche shrinkage/hydration model, you will also need mix‐specific constants b, c (which includes w/c correction), and α‐time relationships; those are not shown here but must be sourced from literature or calibration tests.  
– In practice:  
    • Verify that TEMP is consistent with the calibration data for your maturity or rate model.  
    • Measure or estimate QMAX from adiabatic calorimetry or from published values for similar cementitious systems.  
    • Determine TK by fitting early‐age calorimetric curves to the chosen α(τ) expression.  
    • Choose S by regression against maturity‐strength data if using Saul’s or similar approaches.

The table shown is a fragment of the input‐deck specification for defining PIPE or culvert elements in a finite‐element RAG model. It lists the parameters that must appear on each “PIPE” record (or can be omitted to pick up defaults), together with their meanings, physical units and default‐value markers. Below is a detailed walk-through of its structure:

1. Overall Table Layout  
   • Columns  
     – Item: the keyword or code that identifies a parameter field on the input record.  
     – Description: a brief English explanation of what the parameter controls.  
     – Unit: the physical unit in which the parameter is expressed (if any). A dash “—” means unitless or integer id.  
     – Default: the character token used in the input deck to signal “use the default value” rather than supplying an explicit number.  
   • Rows  
     – Each row corresponds to one of the two required or optional fields (Item = NO, L) on a pipe‐element definition line.

2. Row 1: “NO”  
   • Item = NO  
     – This integer code identifies the element number. It may also be used to group elements into secondary sets for post‐processing or for applying boundary conditions en masse.  
   • Description = “Element number or secondary group”  
     – If you supply a single positive integer, that becomes the unique element identifier in the model topology.  
     – If you repeat the same integer on multiple PIPE records, those elements form a “secondary group” that can be toggled or loaded together (e.g. for switching between open and closed channel conditions).  
   • Unit = “—”  
     – It is unitless: the code simply labels or groups elements.  
   • Default = “!”  
     – The exclamation mark indicates that this field is mandatory. You cannot omit NO; every PIPE line must begin with a valid element number or group code.

3. Row 2: “L”  
   • Item = L  
     – This floating‐point value sets the “effective length” of the pipe or open channel segment.  
     – It overrides the nodal spacing when the hydraulic length differs from the geometric distance between the upstream and downstream nodes. Typical reasons include accounting for fittings, bends or culvert entrance/exit losses.  
   • Description = “Effective length of pipe or channel if not equal the distance between nodes”  
     – If L is omitted, the code assumes the straight‐line distance between the node coordinates.  
   • Unit = m  
     – Must be entered in metres.  
   • Default = “*”  
     – The star character tells the solver to use the nodal‐distance default rather than a user‐supplied override. If you want to specify L explicitly, replace “*” with a numeric value in metres.

4. How This Connects to the Broader PIPE Element Definition  
   – In its simplest form (a straight, circular pipe with uniform roughness), you define a TUBE section, providing just NO, L, MEXT (the roughness), and possibly diameter. For more complex polygons (open channels, manholes), you’d see additional records (e.g. VERT segments, EXP entries for edge‐by‐edge roughness).  
   – Before running a full‐flow (Prandtl–Colebrook) or open‐channel (Darcy–Weisbach) hydraulic simulation, ensure you set TURB=1 and KITE=1 in CTRL.  
   – See also LINK records (to connect pipe elements to junctions or manifolds) and SECT definitions (to choose between tube, polygon or arbitrary cross‐section shapes).

This table defines the two fundamental fields required for every “loading case” (LC) record in the database.  In the broader context of structural‐analysis input decks, each analysis step or load combination is tagged by one LC record—no more, no less.  Subsequent blocks (surface loads, boundary conditions, special functions) all refer back to that LC number.  Optionally, one can introduce an initial state as a “parent” LC (using record PLC) and then record only the difference between that parent and the new loading case via the CTRL LDIF offset mechanism.  See also the related tables BOUN (boundary conditions), SURF (surface loads) and FUNC (prescribed functions) for how they tie into LC.

Table structure:
1. Column “Item”  
   – Identifies the keyword or code used in the input deck.  In this case, the two legal keywords for LC are NO and TITL.  
2. Column “Description”  
   – Explains the semantic meaning of each keyword.  
3. Column “Unit”  
   – Indicates the data type or units expected by the parser.  A dash “–” means no physical unit; Lit32 means a literal ASCII string of up to 32 characters.  
4. Column “Default”  
   – Supplies the value assumed if the user omits that field.

Row details:
• NO  
  – Description: “Number of the case.”  This integer uniquely identifies the loading case within the current analysis data base.  It ties together all related BOUN, SURF, FUNC, etc., entries that belong to the same stage of the simulation.  
  – Unit: none (the parser simply reads an integer).  
  – Default: 1.  If you omit NO, the loader will assign case number 1.  Practically, you should always specify this explicitly to avoid unintended overwriting of case 1 or conflicts when combining multiple blocks.

• TITL  
  – Description: “Designation of the case.”  A short, human‐readable name or title for this loading case, for example “Dead Load,” “Live Load,” or “Thermal Expansion + Pre‐stress.”  
  – Unit: Lit32.  The entry must be an ASCII text string up to 32 characters long.  
  – Default: none.  If you omit TITL, the parser proceeds without a title, but downstream logging and result output will lack a descriptive label for the case.

Usage notes:
– Only one LC record is permitted per input block.  If you include multiple NO/TITL records back to back, only the last will be honored.  
– To define a delta‐load relative to a previously defined case (PLC), you declare the parent case with PLC and then introduce a CTRL LDIF record carrying a positive or negative offset for the LC number.  This mechanism avoids duplication of the entire case description, storing only differences between cases.  
– Every subsequent BOUN, SURF or FUNC command references the active LC number; changing NO in the middle of a block effectively switches the “active load set.”  
– Think of LC as the primary index in the RAG (resource‐action‐geometry) vector store: it groups all actions (loads, supports, boundary conditions) that should be evaluated together in one analysis run.

The table presented defines the input parameters for the generic BOUN record, which is used to assign boundary conditions (potential, flow, mixed/convective) to a selected set of nodes in a finite‐element mesh.  Each row in the table corresponds to one input “item” (keyword), its meaning (“Description”), the physical or logical unit it carries (“Unit”) and the default value assumed when that item is omitted (“Default”).  Below is a detailed walkthrough of each parameter, followed by contextual notes on how they interact with the various BOUN‐type boundary conditions (H, HP, QA, SPEC, etc.).

1.  TYPE  
    • Description: Specifies which kind of boundary condition is being defined.  
    • Unit: Literal (LIT) keyword.  
    • Default: QA (quantity inflow/outflow).  
    • Context: Valid TYPEs include H (potential/head/temperature), HP (conditional potential with seepage check), QA/QAD (external flow), I/QID (internal flow), SPEC (mixed/convective), etc.  This key determines how VAL and other parameters are interpreted.

2.  VAL  
    • Description: The numerical value driving the boundary condition. What “VAL” means depends on TYPE:  
      – H/HP: prescribed potential (e.g. head in m or temperature in K).  
      – QA/QAD: volumetric flow rate (positive = inflow, negative = outflow).  
      – SPEC: conductivity (e.g. l/sec/m or W/K per unit boundary length).  
    • Unit: “*” (generic numerical).  
    • Default: “!” (must be supplied by user; no built‐in default).

3.  FROM  
    • Description: Starting node number (or literal). Can also be EDGE or QGRP.  
    • Unit: – or LIT.  
    • Default: 1.  
    • Context: Combined with TO and INC to generate a sequence of node IDs, or use FROM = EDGE/‘UP’/QGRP to select entire edges or quadrilateral element groups.

4.  TO  
    • Description: End node number of the selection.  
    • Unit: –  
    • Default: same as FROM.  
    • Context: Marks the terminal index when choosing a numeric range of nodes.

5.  INC  
    • Description: Increment or selection type when building the node list.  
    • Unit: – or LIT.  
    • Default: 1.  
    • Context: A positive integer for step size, or “FIT” to interpolate nodes on an edge.

6.  F  
    • Description: Transient condition function number (links to FUNC record).  
    • Unit: –  
    • Default: 0 (steady‐state).

7.  VP  
    • Description: Auxiliary parameter, interpreted per TYPE:  
      – HP: suction limit (negative pore pressure) before potential correction. Default preset to –9999 for free‐surface checks.  
      – SPEC: environmental potential (ambient head or temperature).  
    • Unit: m (or K for thermal).  
    • Default: 0.0.

8.  EPS  
    • Description: Emissivity ratio, only for SPEC (radiative/mixed).  
    • Unit: –  
    • Default: 0.0.  
    • Context: Appears in the Stefan–Boltzmann term EPS·5.67E–8·(H⁴–VP⁴).

9.  NB  
    • Description: Balance number — controls iterative balancing of flows (QA/I/QAD/QID) or disables seepage‐check when negative or zero.  
    • Unit: m/K (for potential types) or integer group ID for internal flows.  
    • Default: 0.0.

10. DVX, DVY, DVZ  
    • Description: Global gradient components applied to the boundary value, so that for any node at coordinates (X,Y,Z):  
        VAL(node) = VAL + DVX·X + DVY·Y + DVZ·Z  
    • Unit: “*”/m (i.e. unitless per meter).  
    • Default: 0.0 for each.

Contextual Notes on BOUN Types  
– H: All selected nodes receive a fixed potential equal to VAL (possibly offset by an initial field if F>0).  
– HP: Potential enforced only if resulting pressure is positive; otherwise a free‐seepage condition (H = –z) is imposed. NB ≤ 0 disables the seepage‐check altogether.  
– QA/QAD and I/QID: Define point or line inflow/outflow rates per unit time (internal vs. external accounting). QAD/QID refer rates to element edge length. NB may specify the group for internal balances. When NB>0, the well‐type logic iteratively adjusts water‐level so total flow matches VAL, with VP limiting suction.  
– SPEC: Mixed (e.g. convective + radiative) boundary. The nodal flux is Q = −(H−VP)·VAL + EPS·5.67E−8·(H⁴−VP⁴). Equivalent mechanically to a spring (conductivity VAL) with support displacement VP, plus a nonlinear radiation term via EPS.

1. Context and Standards  
   - These values are typical surface heat‐transfer coefficients combining convection and radiation effects.

   • Outer side of ceilings and walls  
     – Description: The ambient‐side surface of horizontal and vertical elements exposed to outside air under normal conditions.

The table shown is the parameter‐definition block for a generic boundary‐condition record (SURF, QAS, QIS, QAV, QIV, SPEC, etc.) in our RAG‐ready data model.  Each row names one keyword (“Item”), explains its role (“Description”), gives its physical or logical unit (“Unit”), and states the default value if that keyword is omitted (“Default”).  Below is a field‐by‐field breakdown:

1.  TYPE  
   • Description: A literal identifier that selects which boundary‐condition applies.  Valid codes include QAS, QIS (surface inflow/outflow), QAV, QIV (volume‐referenced), SPEC (mixed/convective), and any other user‐defined record names (see LC, BOUN references).  
   • Unit: LIT (i.e. a string token)  
   • Default: “!” (missing—must be supplied)

2.  VAL  
   • Description: The magnitude of the boundary effect.  Interpretation depends on TYPE:  
     – For QAS/QIS: flux in quantity-units/m² per time-unit; positive=net inflow, negative=net outflow.  
     – For QAV/QIV: volumetric rate in quantity-units/m³ per time-unit.  
     – For SPEC: the convective coefficient (e.g. l/sec/m or W/K per area), used in Q = –(H–VP)·VAL + EPS·5.67E–8·(H⁴–VP⁴).  
   • Unit: “*” (unit depends on context, see system record SYST for time‐unit and material units)  
   • Default: “!” (mandatory)

3.  FROM  
   • Description: The starting element number (or group-id) to which this BC applies.  If the literal GRP is used instead of a quad element list, FROM can be the primary‐group number or a secondary‐group identifier.  
   • Unit: –/LIT (either an integer index or a literal group tag)  
   • Default: 1

4.  TO  
   • Description: The ending element number of the range.  All elements between FROM and TO (inclusive), stepping by INC, receive the same condition.  If omitted, TO = FROM.  
   • Unit: – (integer)  
   • Default: FROM

5.  INC  
   • Description: Increment step between element indices.  Allows you to assign the BC to every nth element in [FROM,TO].  
   • Unit: – (integer)  
   • Default: 1

6.  F  
   • Description: Transient‐condition function index.  Refers to a time‐series definition in the FUNC record.  When non‐zero, VAL is modulated over time.  
   • Unit: – (integer index into FUNC table)  
   • Default: 0 (i.e. steady‐state)

7.  VP  
   • Description: Environment potential for mixed/convective boundary (SPEC).  In hydraulics VP is a head [m]; in thermal problems VP is temperature [K].  
   • Unit: m/K  
   • Default: 0.0

8.  EPS  
   • Description: Emissivity or radiation‐exchange coefficient in SPEC conditions.  Used together with VAL to compute net radiative flux via the Stefan–Boltzmann term EPS·5.67E–8·(H⁴–VP⁴).  
   • Unit: – (dimensionless ratio)  
   • Default: 0.0

9.  NB  
   • Description: Balance‐account number.  For internal‐inflow (QIS, QIV) this selects which mass or energy balance the quantity is credited to.  
   • Unit: – (integer)  
   • Default: 1

Usage notes and cross‐references:  
 • Records SURF, QAV and QIV apply to quadrilateral surface elements or volume elements specified by TYPE.  QAS/QIS only reference surface facets; QAV/QIV only volume.  
 • The SYST record defines the time‐unit scale (seconds, hours, etc.) used by all “per time” rates in VAL.  
 • The BOUN record (see separate documentation) gives a master listing of SPEC parameters and how EPS, VP and VAL interact with node‐based potentials H.  
 • When specifying a literal group (GRP) at FROM, TO is interpreted as group id or secondary grouping, not an element index.  

By indexing these nine fields into a vector store, an RAG system can quickly retrieve “what does INC do in a QAS record?” or “which parameter controls the radiation term in SPEC?” while leveraging the contextual cross‐pointers (FUNC, SYST, BOUN) embedded in the table.
