The table summarizes the parameters that define a time‐dependent boundary or surface function (record “​FUNC​”) in a transient analysis. Each row corresponds to one of the four items you must supply when you build a FUNC record. In practice, one or more FUNC records are referenced by BOUN (boundary) or SURF (surface) entries—or by LC load cases—whenever a time‐varying condition is needed.

1. Item: T  
   – Description: Time value  
   – Unit: “*” (this means the same time unit you’ve selected globally via the SYST record)  
   – Default: “!” (no default: you must explicitly specify a time stamp)  
   – Notes:  
     • Each function consists of at least two (T, F) pairs sharing the same function number.  
     • Time values must be sorted in ascending order.  
     • For t < T₁ or t > Tₙ (the first or last time point), the function factor is assumed zero.

2. Item: F  
   – Description: Function value or predefined type  
   – Unit: “–” when numeric or “LIT” when a literal preset curve is selected  
   – Default: “!” (mandatory)  
   – Allowed literals (case‐sensitive) for design‐fire curves (per EC1-2 §4.2):  
     • ISO — standard “ISO‐fire” curve (eq. 3.8):  
         T(t) = 20 + 345 · log10(8 t + 1)  
     • EXT — external fire curve (eq. 3.9):  
         T(t) = 20 + 660 · [1 – 0.687 e^(–0.32 t) – 0.313 e^(–3.8 t)]  
     • CARB — hydrocarbon fire curve (eq. 3.10):  
         T(t) = 20 + 1080 · [1 – 0.325 e^(–0.167 t) – 0.675 e^(–2.5 t)]  
   – Notes:  
     • If you omit FUNC altogether, BOUN or SURF values remain constant in time.  
     • When defining a SPEC‐type boundary, only the potential (VP) is multiplied by the function; in that case set VP = 1.0 and let FUNC supply the time‐history.

3. Item: NO  
   – Description: Number of the time function (function index)  
   – Unit: “–” (integer)  
   – Default: 1  
   – Notes:  
     • This index groups multiple (T, F) records into one coherent time‐history curve.  
     • You may have many FUNC definitions (NO = 1, 2, 3, …), each with its own T/F pairs.

4. Item: TITL  
   – Description: Title of this function  
   – Unit: Lit32 (up to 32 characters of text)  
   – Default: “–” (optional)  
   – Notes:  
     • Use TITL to document the purpose or name of the function (e.g., “Fire Load Curve”, “Ramp‐up Cooling”).  
     • No default string is inserted if you omit this field.

Cross‐References:  
• LC: associates a load case with one or more FUNC definitions via boundary or surface IDs.  
• BOUN / SURF: reference FUNC by the NO index to impose time‐varying fluxes, temperatures, or potentials.  

In sum, the table defines the minimal set of fields to build a transient function record (FUNC). You must supply at least two (T,F) entries sharing the same NO index; values outside the defined time span default to zero. Alternatively, you may select one of three predefined fire‐curve literals (ISO, EXT, CARB) to capture standard temperature‐vs.‐time histories without discrete point‐by‐point data.

The image is a hand-drawn, schematic time-history plot of a general “transient function” F used in boundary‐condition definitions (see FUNC in the additional context). The horizontal axis is time, marked at four key instants t1, t2, t3 and t4; the vertical axis is the function magnitude, labeled F. A caption beneath the sketch reads “Figure 3.8: Transient function.” No numerical scales are shown, so the emphasis is purely on the qualitative, piecewise‐linear shape of the function over time.

Starting from time zero up to t1, the function value F remains at zero (or some baseline), drawn as a horizontal line along the time axis. At t1, the function begins a linear ramp: between t1 and t2, F increases steadily, resulting in an upward-sloping segment that peaks exactly at t2. A vertical line is drawn at t2 to emphasize the end of the rising segment and the start of a new interval. From t2 to t3, the function decreases linearly; this segment slopes downward from the peak value at t2 to an intermediate level at t3. At t3, a shorter, steeper vertical drop brings F down to a lower plateau. Finally, from t3 to t4 (and beyond), F remains constant at that lower value, indicated by a horizontal line segment extending to and past t4.

Key graphical features:
• Zero baseline (t=0 to t1): F is constant at zero.  
• Ramp up (t1 to t2): Linear increase in F, reaching a maximum at t2.  
• Ramp down (t2 to t3): Linear decrease from peak to an intermediate value.  
• Step down (at t3): Abrupt drop to a lower level, then constant through t4.  

In the context of a finite-element transient analysis record (FUNC), such a piecewise‐linear curve would be defined by at least two (time, value) pairs for each segment, sorted by ascending time. Before the first specified time (t1) and after the last (t4), the function is assumed zero unless a literal design-fire curve is selected instead (for example, the ISO-fire, external fire or hydrocarbon curves defined in EC1-2 §4.2). When associated with a BOUN or SURF boundary condition, the function values shown here would multiply the prescribed boundary value at each time. For a SPEC type (voltage or potential), only the VP‐value would be scaled, which is why VP is often set to 1.0 in tandem with a FUNC definition. This sketch thus provides a clear, visual template for a transient, time-dependent boundary multiplier in thermal, structural or other multiphysics simulations.

The image is a black-and-white, two-dimensional line plot titled at the bottom “Figure 3.9: Design Fires.” It presents three smooth, time-temperature curves that illustrate three standardized “design fire” scenarios (ISO fire, external fire, hydrocarbon fire) as defined by EC1-2 (equations 3.8–3.10).  

Axes and Tick Marks  
• Horizontal axis (x-axis) runs from 0 to 80 in uniform steps of 5 (labelled “0,” “5,00,” “10,0,” “15,0,” … up to “80,0”). These represent elapsed time (presumably in minutes) used in transient heat analyses.  
• Vertical axis (y-axis) runs from 50 up to 1 100 in increments of 50 (labels at 50, 100, 150, … 1 100). These are temperature values in degrees Celsius.  
• Both axes are drawn with simple solid lines. Tick marks are relatively long and project inward; there is no grid. Axis labels and numbers are set in a plain, small serif font.  

Three Curves  
1. ISO-Fire Curve (Equation 3.8)  
   – Starts near the bottom of the plot and rises sharply during the first few minutes.  
   – Levels off at approximately 650 °C by t ≈ 10 min and remains essentially flat thereafter.  
   – Appears as the lowest plateau among the three curves.  

2. External-Fire Curve (Equation 3.9)  
   – Climbs more gradually than the ISO curve, with a smooth convex shape.  
   – At t = 80 min it approaches about 950 °C (midway between the ISO plateau and the hydrocarbon peak).  
   – Lies between the other two curves throughout most of the time axis.  

3. Hydrocarbon-Fire Curve (Equation 3.10)  
   – Exhibits the steepest initial rise, rapidly gaining temperature in the first 5–10 min.  
   – Levels off just below 1 100 °C by around t ≈ 15 min, forming the topmost curve.  
   – Maintains a nearly horizontal plateau for the remainder of the period.  

Caption and Context  
• Below the plot, aligned to the right, is the legend or caption “Figure 3.9: Design Fires.”  
• No in-plot legend or curve labels are shown; the correspondence to ISO, external, and hydrocarbon fire curves is implied by the caption and the three standard equations (3.8–3.10) in the surrounding text.  
• The curves exemplify how a FUNC record in a transient analysis can be used to impose time-varying boundary conditions (e.g. temperature on a surface). Each fire curve is a predefined function (literal or piecewise) that multiplies a base BOUN or SURF value when simulating design fire exposure.

 FUNC
 The record FUNC describes a boundary condition which changes in time during a transient analysis. The time values are expected in the unit specified at record SYST. The table shown is the parameter‐definition block for the COPY command (used, for example, to recombine wind‐pressure result cases into a single case or to convert nodal pressures into pressure coefficients).  COPY does not require a HYDRA license.  Below is a structured, field-by-field description of every row and column in the table, together with how these fields tie back to the accompanying explanatory text.

1.  Columns in the Table  
    •  Item  
       –  The keyword or parameter name to be supplied on the COPY command line.  
    •  Description  
       –  A concise explanation of what each parameter does.  
    •  Unit  
       –  The physical unit or type of the parameter.  A dash (—) means “unitless” in this context.  An asterisk (*) indicates that the value acts as a multiplier or divisor on existing nodal pressures.  
    •  Default  
       –  The value assumed if the user does not explicitly supply one.

2.  Rows (Parameters)  

    A.  FROM  
        –  Description: “Range of result cases to be treated.”  When you invoke COPY you often want to process a block of existing load‐case results.  FROM specifies the first (lower) case number in that block.  
        –  Unit: — (unitless index)  
        –  Default: – (no default; you must supply FROM when calling COPY)  

    B.  TO  
        –  Description: “Range of result cases to be treated.”  TO gives the last (upper) case number in the range.  COPY will read every result case from FROM through TO, inclusive.  
        –  Unit: —  
        –  Default: –  

    C.  TARG  
        –  Description: “Resulting case number.”  This is the single, consolidated case in which all the processed results will be written.  For example, you might collect five wind‐pressure cases (cases 101–105) and store the combined pressure‐coefficient result in case 201.  
        –  Unit: —  
        –  Default: –  

    D.  PCOR  
        –  Description: “Correction of pressures by a value to add.”  This parameter allows you to shift all nodal pressure results by a constant offset.  It is useful if you need to normalize against a reference pressure or to convert from absolute to gauge pressure, etc.  
        –  Unit: * (acts as an additive correction on the pressure field)  
        –  Default: 0.0 (no additive correction if the user omits PCOR)  

    E.  PREF  
        –  Description: “Correction of pressures by a reference to divide.”  Sometimes you want to scale your pressures—e.g., to non-dimensionalize them by a reference pressure.  PREF is the divisor applied to each nodal pressure after the additive correction.  
        –  Unit: * (scaling factor)  
        –  Default: 1.0 (no scaling if the user omits PREF)  

3.  How This Relates to the Broader Workflow  
    •  HIST versus COPY:  
       –  HIST is used to store time-histories (potentials, temperatures, fluxes) for transient analysis.  You select nodes or element groups and then call HIST to dump their time development into the database.  HIST REST will pick up an existing selection set and continue building the time history.  
       –  COPY is unrelated to time‐history.  Instead, it is a post-processing utility for nodal results.  It merges, offsets, and/or rescales existing result cases into a new one.  
    •  Practical Example (Wind Pressures):  
       –  Suppose PHYSICA has generated a series of wind‐pressure result cases 300–305.  You want pressure coefficients Cp = (p – p_ref)/q_ref.  You might call:  
            COPY FROM 300 TO 305 TARG 350 PCOR –p_ref PREF q_ref  
         This loops through cases 300–305, subtracts p_ref from each pressure (PCOR = –p_ref), divides by dynamic pressure q_ref (PREF = q_ref), and writes the average or combined result into case 350.  

4.  Important Notes  
    –  All four of the FROM, TO, TARG, PCOR/PREF keywords are optional in terms of ordering, but FROM, TO, and TARG are mandatory semantically.  
    –  Unspecified PCOR or PREF revert to their defaults (0.0 additive and 1.0 divisive), meaning COPY will simply copy raw pressures if you do not ask for corrections.  
    –  COPY will not generate any additional nodal or elemental data beyond what it is pointed at—so you must have run a prior analysis step and created the source cases before invoking COPY.

HIST
 For transient analysis there are either the method to save the complete results for any time step at a different load case number or to select some important results like potentials, temperature or flux quantities of elements or groups (max 1024) and to save their development in time in a compact form in the database. DYNR will then be used to show these diagrams
 If a selection set has already been established for the primary load case, a definition of HIST REST will take this and continue with the time history automatically.
 COPY – Modify nodal results in the database

 COPY is a command for special cases where separate result cases should be combined to a single one. For the evaluation of wind pressures which have been calculated with PHYSICA, the conversion to pressure coefficients is a useful aid.

The table under review defines the four key “IMPO” parameters that drive the import of external result data into HYDRA.  In the context of the IMPO option (which does not require a HYDRA license), users prepare a plain-text file containing node-value pairs, interspersed with optional comment lines (beginning “$” or “#”), optional time stamps (“*TIME=…”), and a terminating “*END”.  The table below lays out each IMPO keyword, its meaning, acceptable units, and default settings.

1. LC  
   • Description: “Number of result case.”  
     – This integer index tells HYDRA which result set or case number from your external data to associate with the subsequent values.  
   • Unit: none (—)  
   • Default: user must supply (“!” indicates “mandatory”)

2. TYPE  
   • Description: “Type of results.” HYDRA expects you to declare what physical quantity is being imported. Three literal (LIT) options are allowed:  
     – TEMK: temperatures in Kelvin  
     – TEMP: temperatures in Celsius  
     – TK2C: instructs HYDRA to convert Kelvin readings in the file into Celsius on import  
   • Unit: LIT (literal text string)  
   • Default: mandatory  

   Notes:  
   – If you specify TYPE=TEMK, HYDRA reads the raw numbers as Kelvin.  
   – If you choose TEMP, it assumes the file already carries Celsius values.  
   – TK2C is a convenience flag for files in Kelvin, automatically applying (K–273.15) conversion.

3. T  
   • Description: “Time value.”  
     – This floating-point or integer entry tags the entire block of node data with its corresponding simulation time.  
     – When importing a series of transient (time-dependent) results, use a distinct *TIME record in the file; this T parameter aligns with that tag.  
   • Unit: sec (seconds)  
   • Default: mandatory

4. FROM  
   • Description: “Name of external file to import.”  
     – A literal text string (file path or filename) that points HYDRA at your prepared import file.  
     – Can include relative or absolute path syntax, depending on your working directory and system conventions.  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: mandatory

How It Fits Together  
• A valid IMPO block in your HYDRA input deck looks like this (example):
     LC    1  
     TYPE  TEMK  
     T     10.0  
     FROM  results_t=10.dat  
     *END  

• The external file results_t=10.dat might begin with comments:
     $ this file contains temperature at time = 10 s  
     *TIME=10.0  
     1   295.0  
     2   300.5  
     3   302.3  
     …  
     *END  

• HYDRA reads “LC=1” and tags the imported dataset as result case #1.  
• It interprets each numeric line as a (node,temperature) pair, using Kelvin units (TEMK) and matching them to the declared time (T=10 s).  
• No additional HYDRA license is required to use these IMPO directives.

Summary  
This table provides a concise reference for all mandatory IMPO parameters—LC, TYPE, T, FROM—plus the three allowed result‐type literals.  By adhering to the units and literal conventions (LIT) and terminating each import block with *END, users can seamlessly feed outside results into HYDRA’s post-processing framework.

IMPO
 With IMPO it is possible to import results from other programs into HYDRA. The import file is a text file and may contain any comments starting with a $ or #, the data values have to be specified in lines each containing the node number and the data value at this node in free format.
 A line *END terminates the import, a line *TIME=timevalue may be used to structure a transient result file.

The table under review defines two key input parameters—OPT and VAL—that together control both the *categories* of data written out by a solver (via OPT) and the *verbosity level* of that output (via VAL). It is organized into four columns:

•  Item  
•  Description  
•  Unit  
•  Default  

1.  Item = OPT  
    – Unit: LIT (literal string)  
    – Default: “FULL”  
    – Description: selects which *types* of results are written to output; you may list any combination of the following tokens (separated by blanks):  
       •  FULL  – include *all* available output categories  
       •  NODE  – nodal coordinates and nodal solution values  
       •  ELEM  – element connectivity, geometry, or element‐level results  
       •  FUNC  – user‐defined functional values (any post‐processing functions you have specified)  
       •  BOUN  – boundary‐condition definitions and responses  
       •  POT   – potentials (e.g. electric or scalar field values) or temperatures  
       •  QUAN  – derived physical quantities (stresses, strains, fluxes if not covered by VELO)  
       •  VELO  – fluxes, velocities, or field gradients  
       •  STAT  – iterative solver statistics, convergence histories, residual norms  
       •  STEP  – transient‐analysis time‐step headers and time‐history blocks  

    By combining these tokens you can precisely tailor which data blocks appear in the output file.  If you omit OPT or specify “FULL”, every available category will be written.  

2.  Item = VAL  
    – Unit: LIT  
    – Default: “FULL”  
    – Description: sets the *amount* of output for the categories chosen with OPT.  You may use either the numeric code or its mnemonic equivalent:  
       •  –1 or OFF   – do *not* perform the requested computation or write any output  
       •   0 or NO    – perform any internal computations but suppress all output blocks  
       •   1 or YES   – regular output (minimal, essential information)  
       •   2 or FULL  – extensive output (every detail that solver records, including intermediate data)  
       •   3 or EXTR  – extreme output (maximum verbosity; e.g. full iteration‐by‐iteration history, all auxiliary arrays)  

    Common invocation:  
       •  ECHO 3  or  ECHO EXTR   — sets VAL to its highest verbosity level for debugging or detailed post‐processing.  
       •  ECHO 1  or  ECHO YES    — for standard, concise output.  
       •  ECHO –1 or ECHO OFF    — to turn off this entire output system.  

Additional context:  
– “ECHO” is the command that ties together OPT and VAL in your input deck.  
– Chapter 4 of the manual describes in detail how each verbosity level (particularly EXTR) expands every output section, often to support in‐depth troubleshooting or development of custom post‐processors.  
– In practice, you first list the categories via OPT, then immediately follow with VAL to set how much detail each category will emit.  

This two-parameter design provides maximum flexibility: you decide both *what* gets written and *how much* of it. The default state (OPT=FULL, VAL=FULL) means “write everything in extensive form,” which is often more than needed for routine analysis but invaluable when you must audit or validate every step of the solution process.

Below is a systematic breakdown of the “CROSS SECTIONS” table, showing how it is structured and what every field means. You can use this description when ingesting the table into a RAG-style vector store so that both the hierarchy and the semantics of each column are preserved.

1. Overall Organization  
   - The table is grouped by a primary “section number” (No).  
   - For each section No you will always see one “summary row,” followed by one or more “element rows” and, if requested via an ECHO SECT EXTR command, “vertex rows.”  
   - Commands:  
     • ECHO SECT FULL  → expands each section into its partial‐section elements  
     • ECHO SECT EXTR  → further expands each element into its individual vertices  

2. Column Definitions  
   • No   : Cross-section identifier (integer). All rows for that same section share this value.  
   • PNO  : Partial‐section index (integer). On summary rows this is blank; on element rows it numbers each partial subsection.  
   • VNO  : Vertex index (integer). Only present on vertex rows (EXTR); otherwise blank.  
   • area [m2]    : Cross-sectional area.  
   • CIRCUM [m]   : Wetted perimeter (total internal perimeter of flow area).  
   • EFFECT. [m]  : Hydraulic effective radius (area / perimeter).  
   • K [mm]       : Mean roughness height of the section or element.  
   • LEAKAGE [m2/sec] : Leakage coefficient (rate of leakage per unit time).  
   • Y [m]        : Horizontal coordinate. On summary rows this may carry special flags (e.g. “S” for slope), on elements it’s the centroid’s Y.  
   • Z [m]        : Vertical coordinate (invert or centroid elevation).  

3. Row Types and Their Roles  
   A. Summary Rows (only No populated)  
     – Provides the total sectional area, total circumference, overall hydraulic radius, plus the mean K and leakage for the entire section.  
     – Example:  
         No=2  area=57.0000 m2  CIRCUM=59.301 m  EFFECT.=31.301 m  K=4.9 mm  LEAKAGE=1.55E+02 m2/s  Y=S  Z=-12.5  
       Here “S” in Y signals a section flag; Z gives an overall reference elevation.  

   B. Element Rows (No + PNO populated)  
     – Break the section into geometric “partials” (e.g. left bank, invert, right bank).  
     – Each element has its own area, perimeter, effective radius, roughness and leakage, plus the centroid coordinates (Y,Z).  
     – Example:  
         No=2  PNO=1  area=6.5000 m2  CIRCUM=15.414 m  EFFECT.=8.414 m  K=12.6 mm  LEAKAGE=2.54E+01 m2/s  Y=15.000 m  Z=-2.000 m  

   C. Vertex Rows (No + PNO + VNO populated)  
     – When you request ECHO SECT EXTR, each element is further detailed as a closed polygon.  
     – Columns area, CIRCUM, EFFECT, K and LEAKAGE are blank (not applicable).  
     – Y and Z give the coordinates of each vertex in sequence.  
     – Example sequence for partial section PNO=1:  
         VNO=2  Y=20.0 m  Z=-1.0 m  
         VNO=3  Y=12.0 m  Z=-1.0 m  
         VNO=4  Y=-8.0 m  Z=-2.0 m  

4. Hierarchical Keying for a Vector Store  
   – Primary key: section No  
   – Secondary key: element PNO (ECHO SECT FULL)  
   – Tertiary key: vertex VNO (ECHO SECT EXTR)  
   – Store each row as a document with metadata fields: {No, PNO, VNO, area, CIRCUM, EFFECT, K, LEAKAGE, Y, Z}  
   – You can then retrieve by section and drill down to elements or raw geometry as needed.  

By faithfully preserving the three‐tier hierarchy and annotating each row with its function (summary, element, or vertex), you enable fine‐grained retrievals—whether you need the overall hydraulic properties or the exact polygonal coordinates of the cross section.

   1. H1 (“Header lines”)  
      • Role: Controls the thickness of the primary header lines that usually span the top of a chart or page.  
      • Unit: cm  
      • Default: 0.35 cm  
      • Special Behavior:  
          – For smaller page or viewport formats, the system will “correct” this default value automatically so that labels can still accommodate up to 72 characters in width without truncation or overlap.  
          – If set explicitly to 0.0 cm, the header lines (and associated labeling) are completely suppressed.  
          – Persistence: Once defined, the H1 value remains in effect until another call redefines either the overall “SIZE” parameter or SCHH itself.  

   2. H2 (“Texts within the legend”)  
      • Role: Governs the font size or line thickness for all text elements inside the chart legend.  
      • Unit: cm  
      • Default: 0.25 cm  

   3. H3 (“Designation of axis”)  
      • Role: Sets the size/weight of the labels used to designate each axis (e.g., “X” or “Y” axis names or units).  
      • Unit: cm  
      • Default: 0.25 cm  

   4. H4 (“Scaling of Axis”)  
      • Role: Defines the size of numeric scale markings and tick-mark labels along each axis.  
      • Unit: cm  
      • Default: 0.25 cm  

   5. H5 (“Company and Program name”)  
      • Role: Determines the line thickness or text size used for a footer block that displays the company name and program identifier/source.  
      • Unit: cm  
      • Default: 0.18 cm  

3. Contextual Note on SCHH  
   • SCHH is the routine or setting under which these “H-line” parameters are grouped.  
   • The defaults listed above apply to all subsequent plots until an explicit SCHH redefinition or a SIZE adjustment is issued.  
   • By centralizing these header-and-text dimensions, users can ensure consistent typographic hierarchy and spacing across multiple visual outputs.

4. Usage Implications for RAG/Vectors  
   • These parameters serve as high-level style tokens. When querying a knowledge base about how to generate a chart or interpret one, an intelligent agent can reference “H1=0.35 cm” to infer nominal header thickness or “H2=0.25 cm” for legend font size.  
   • The special override/suppression rule for H1 (i.e. 0.0 → no header lines) should be flagged as a conditional branch in any generation or analysis workflow.  
   • Persistence semantics (remaining active until SIZE or SCHH redefinition) are crucial for chaining multiple plot commands without repeatedly specifying the same style parameters.

By capturing these details in your vector store—parameter codes, descriptions, units, defaults, special cases, and persistence rules—downstream applications can reliably retrieve both the numeric defaults and the behavioral rules needed to assemble or interpret charts in this system.

Below is a structured, field-by-field breakdown of the input table—suitable for indexing in a RAG/vector store—and a summary of the supplemental “FUNC” context. Each entry covers the parameter name, its purpose, data type or unit, default-value semantics, and any special processing rules.  

1. Field: T  
   – Description: “Time value.” Represents the simulation or measurement time at which a function value is specified.  
   – Unit: seconds (sec).  
   – Default marker: “!” (exclamation mark) indicates this field is mandatory for each new data record (cannot be omitted on the very first entry).  
   – Notes:  
     • If no explicit T value is provided on subsequent lines, the system will automatically take the most recent ΔT (DT) and add it to the prior time stamp.  
     • In uniformly spaced time-step scenarios, you may omit T entirely after the initial entry—DT alone suffices to advance time.  

2. Field: F  
   – Description: “Function value.” This is the actual data point or simulated quantity being recorded at time T.  
   – Unit: dimensionless (—). The unit depends entirely on how you define the function in DYNR (e.g., temperature, pressure, velocity).  
   – Default marker: “!” — mandatory on every line where a new function sample is being recorded.  
   – Notes:  
     • You can define any number of user-specific functions in DYNR (via the FUNC statement) and reference them here.  
     • F values drive the HIST display comparisons; every recorded time-step must include an F.  

3. Field: DT  
   – Description: “Division of time.” Specifies the increment (in seconds) to advance from the prior time stamp when T is omitted or to override the default time‐step.  
   – Unit: seconds (sec).  
   – Default marker: “*” (asterisk) indicates that, if DT is not explicitly given, the system will reuse the last non-zero DT value.  
   – Notes:  
     • First record usually defines DT implicitly via the first two T values (if given).  
     • Ideal for constant‐step runs where specifying T each time would be redundant.  

4. Field: NO  
   – Description: “Number of function.” An integer index that identifies which defined DYNR function (via FUNC) this record pertains to.  
   – Unit: none (—).  
   – Default marker: “*”—optional after the first occurrence.  
   – Notes:  
     • NO and TITL are only processed (evaluated) on the very first data record. On later lines, they remain in force from the initial line.  
     • If you omit NO on line 2+, the last NO is assumed.  

5. Field: TITL  
   – Description: “Designation.” A literal‐string label (up to 24 characters) assigned to this function or curve.  
   – Unit / Data type: Lit24 (24-character literal).  
   – Default marker: implied “*”—optional after the first record.  
   – Notes:  
     • Acts as a human-readable title in plots or HIST tables.  
     • Only the first record’s TITL is parsed; subsequent records inherit it automatically.  

Supplemental Context (FUNC statement)  
• Within the DYNR environment, users invoke a “FUNC” statement to define arbitrary functions (e.g., time-dependent forcing, custom response curves) to be compared by the HIST display routines.  
• Once a FUNC is in place, the “F” column in the table refers directly to its output. This makes the table format highly flexible—any computed or experimental signal can be slotted in.  
• The “NO” index ties a particular column of “F” values back to one of these named FUNC definitions, while “TITL” carries the descriptive legend used in post-processing plots or tables.  

Usage Pattern  
– Line 1 (initial): must specify T, F, NO, TITL (DT may follow if time increments are nonuniform)  
– Lines 2+: can omit T (uses prior T + DT), omit NO/TITL (inherit from line 1), but must supply F each time. DT may be included or omitted if constant.  

This design allows concise, clear data input for time‐series or transient simulations, with automatic time‐stepping and inheritance of function indices and titles after the first record.

FUNC

 NO and TITL are evaluated only for the first function value. If no time value is given, the last time increment will be added to the last time value. For regular time steps the time values may be omitted therefore for all higher values.

The table defines the input parameters for the HIST command, which can plot up to six time-variation curves in a single graph. Each curve is specified by a pair of entries: one to select the node or element whose result history you want, and one to assign a color and line style. In addition, two global parameters select which kind of result (potentials, temperatures, fluxes, etc.) is being plotted and into which storage slot the set of curves will be written. Below is a field-by-field breakdown:

1. LCS  
   • Description: “Storage number of curve”  
   • Unit: (none)  
   • Default: must be specified (“!” indicates a required entry)  
   • Notes: An integer index (typically from 1 to 10 or more, depending on your system) that tells HIST into which internal buffer the set of up to six curves will go. If you later issue another HIST with the same LCS, it will overwrite this buffer.

2. TYPE  
   • Description: “Degree of freedom” (see the preceding remarks)  
     – H, QH, QBH, QHPI: nodal or regional potentials / quantities  
     – VQUA, VBRI: velocities in QUAD / BRIC elements  
     – T, QT, QBT, QTPI: temperatures and heat fluxes at nodes, regions, or links  
     – QQUA, QBRI: heat flux densities in QUAD / BRIC elements  
   • Unit: LIT (literal code identifying the kind of curve requested)  
   • Default: required (“!”)  
   • Notes: Choose the code that matches the physical variable you want to plot. For comparison curves defined by a user function FUNC, put the negative function number here and set LCS to zero.

3. NO1  
   • Description: “First node or element number; Colour and line type of first curve”  
   • Unit: (none)  
   • Default: “–” (no default)  
   • Notes: Enter an integer node or element ID whose history is to be displayed first. In the same field you may append color/line-style codes (e.g. “35,R2”).

4. C1  
   • Description: “Second node or element number”  
   • Unit: (none)  
   • Default: 1001  
   • Notes: If you omit it, HIST assumes you want curve #1’s data repeated for curve #2. You may also add color/line style here.

5. NO2  
   • Description: “Color and line type of second curve”  
   • Unit: (none)  
   • Default: “–”  
   • Notes: Used only if you wish to override the inherited style from C1.

6. C2, NO3, C3, NO4, C4, NO5, C5, NO6  
   • These follow the exact same pattern as C1/NO2:  
     – C2 (third node/element ID; default = C1)  
     – NO3 (color/style for third curve; default = “–”)  
     – C3 (fourth node/element ID; default = C2)  
     – NO4 (color/style for fourth curve; default = “–”)  
     – C4 (fifth node/element ID; default = C3)  
     – NO5 (color/style for fifth curve; default = “–”)  
     – C5 (sixth node/element ID; default = C4)  
     – NO6 (color/style for sixth curve; default = “–”)  

Key behavior:
- If you want fewer than six curves, you can simply omit the later Ci/NOi pairs or leave them blank; they will default to repeating the last specified node ID and retain the same line style (unless a NOi is explicitly set).  
- To plot only user-defined functions (no database-stored histories), set LCS = 0 and give negative function numbers in the NOi positions.  
- The vertical axis range is auto-scaled by default but can be overridden via YMIN/YMAX (or TMIN/TMAX for time axes) in a separate SIZE specification.

The input table defines the set of “types” (physical‐quantity codes) that the HIST command can plot over time. Below is a detailed, column-wise breakdown of its contents, together with the contextual rules that govern how HIST selects and displays these curves.

1. Table Columns  
   • Type Code  
     – A short alphanumeric identifier you pass to HIST (e.g. H, QHPI, VQUA).  
   • Physical Quantity / Element Group  
     – A human-readable description of what each code stands for.  
     – Specifies whether the quantity is associated with nodes, regions, pipes, links, or finite-element types (QUAD, BRIC).  

2. Type Codes and Their Meanings  
   • H  
     – Potentials (e.g. electric or hydraulic potentials at nodes/regions).  
   • QH, QBH, QHPI  
     – Quantities related to “H”:  
       · QH   = total H-quantity per node or region  
       · QBH  = H-quantity per pipe  
       · QHPI = H-quantity at a specified point of interest  
   • VQUA, VBRI  
     – Velocities computed over finite elements:  
       · VQUA = velocity in a QUAD element  
       · VBRI = velocity in a BRIC element  
   • T  
     – Temperature (scalar field at nodes/regions).  
   • QT, QBT, QTPI  
     – Heat-flux quantities:  
       · QT   = total heat flux at nodes or regions  
       · QBT  = heat flux through links or boundaries  
       · QTPI = heat flux at a specified point of interest  
   • QQUA, QBRI  
     – Heat-flux densities in finite elements:  
       · QQUA = flux density in a QUAD element  
       · QBRI = flux density in a BRIC element  

3. Usage Rules & Graph Configuration  
   – HIST allows up to six simultaneous time-variation curves.  
   – By default, HIST determines the Y-axis and time range automatically using the SCALE data (SIZE).  
   – You can manually override the plot range:  
     • YMIN and YMAX to set the vertical axis limits.  
     • TMIN and TMAX to set the time (horizontal) limits.  
   – Comparison curves (user-defined functions) can also be overlaid:  
     • Define a function via FUNC.  
     • To include a function as one of the up-to-six plots, set the corresponding NOi entry to the negative of the function’s index (e.g. NO3 = –2 to plot the 2nd user function).  
     • To plot only comparison curves (no standard HIST curves), set LCS=0.  

4. Practical Tips  
   – Always check that your chosen Type Code matches the physical entity you wish to monitor (nodes vs. elements vs. links).  
   – When combining both database-stored curves and user functions, remember to reserve at least one NOi slot for each function (negative indices).  
   – Use explicit axis limits sparingly; automatic scaling generally provides the best overview unless you need to focus on a narrow band of values.

The table below defines a control block (C6) for customizing the axis‐scale settings of a HIST command plot. If you wish to override those automatic limits, you supply YMIN/YMAX (for the vertical axis) or TMIN/TMAX (for the time axis). TDIM then specifies the time‐unit label and scale for TMIN/TMAX.

Rows / Parameters

2. YMIN  
  – Item: “YMIN”

3. YMAX  
  – Item: “YMAX”

  – Item: “TMAX”
